question: to the Commission Sander Smit (ECR) Subject:

Audit CT-2025-0037, completed in November 2025 and published on 12 February 2026, found that Chinese slaughterhouses did not comply with food safety standards: carcasses with visible faecal contamination were simply rinsed, whereas under EU standards, the meat should have been disposed of immediately. Traceability requirements were found to be so poorly enforced that it could not be determined whether the poultry meat originated from one of the designated production sites. In the three months between the completion and publication of the report, exports to the EU appear to have continued unabated, under a certification system that the Commission had already deemed unreliable at that time. 1.

Why did the Commission not immediately suspend imports pursuant to Article 128 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, and why does the Commission consider the food safety risks associated with the identified deficiencies to be acceptable?

How many tons of Chinese poultry meat entered the EU between the audit and the publication of its findings, and can the Commission provide consumers with information on the Member States, the importers, and the products in which the meat ended up?
On what date did the Commission inform the Member States – in particular the Netherlands as one of the main importing countries – of the findings, and what specific measures were taken in response?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.6.2026) During the audit in China in November 2025 on poultry meat products1, significant deficiencies were identified and addressed with the authorities in a closure meeting. The audit team emphasised concerns about the safety of poultry meat products, particularly in the event of inadequate corrective measures. These concerns were reiterated in follow-up communications, alongside an urgent request to the Chinese authorities for taking prompt remedial actions to key recommendations. The risk of delisting China for these exports was also underscored should the required improvements fail to materialise within the stipulated timeframe. Whilst the Commission maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward food safety risks, the risk management procedure considered several mitigating factors. Under the current EU rules, imports of fresh poultry meat from China are not allowed2. In addition, all poultry meat products from China must be sterilised, except for poultry meat products from the province of Shandong, for which a less severe risk-mitigation treatment3 suffices. The relatively low incidence of RASFF4 notifications pertaining to imports of Chinese poultry meat products further informed the Commission’s evaluation of the risks. In response to the audit findings, China submitted a thorough action plan, detailing both immediate measures and long-term initiatives to address the shortcomings. The Commission assessed it as satisfactory, contingent upon its timely, effective, and rigorous implementation. To ensure compliance, a follow-up audit will be conducted in China in 2026. In 2025, Member States imported 73 000 tonnes of poultry meat products from China. They were informed via the publication of the audit report on 19 February 20265.

1 https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-report/details/4968. 2 http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2021/404/oj. 3 E.g.: minimum core temperature of 70°C. 4 Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed. 5 China CT-2025-0037 - Food Audits and Analysis: https://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit-
